passages.t: John the Baptist prepares the way
passages.happening: Mark opens with a title: this is the beginning of the good news about Jesus. Then, with no birth story, he takes us straight to the desert by the Jordan River. A man named John is calling people to be baptized, that is, washed in the river as a sign that they are turning away from their sins. Crowds walk out from Jerusalem and the towns of Judea to hear him. John says that someone far greater is coming after him.
passages.hearers:
John's clothes would have made a first-century Jew sit up. Camel's hair and a leather belt were how the Bible describes the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). And the last of the Old Testament prophets had promised that God would send Elijah again before the great day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). So John is dressed as a sign: the promised forerunner has arrived.

The place mattered too. The wilderness was where God first led Israel after Egypt, and the Jordan was the river they crossed into the promised land. Going back out to the river was like starting over.

Locusts and wild honey were food the law allowed (Leviticus 11:22), and they were what the land gave for free. John lived on nothing he had to buy.

John says he is not worthy to untie the other man's sandals. Taking off a master's sandals was a servant's job. John is saying he is not even fit to be that man's servant.
passages.ot: Mark's first quotation (verses 2 and 3) joins three Old Testament promises. God's words to Israel in the desert, “I am sending an angel before you” (Exodus 23:20). The promise in Malachi 3:1 of a messenger who “will prepare the way before Me.” And Isaiah 40:3, a voice crying, “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness.” In Isaiah and Malachi, the one coming is the LORD himself. Mark applies those words to Jesus.
passages.hard: Verse 2 says “As it is written in Isaiah the prophet,” but the first lines come from Exodus and Malachi. Many later manuscripts changed the words to ‘in the prophets’, which shows that early copyists noticed it too. The likeliest answer is simple. Jewish writers often named a combined quotation after its best known source, and Isaiah's words about the wilderness are the heart of what Mark wants to say. It is a way of citing, not a slip.
passages.asks: John's whole job was to point away from himself. He drew a crowd and then told it to look at someone else. Ask what in your life is meant to point to Jesus, and whether it does. John's message was also simple: turn around. What would turning around look like for you this week?

passages.happening: Jesus comes from Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, and John baptizes him. As Jesus comes up out of the water, he sees the sky split open and the Spirit of God coming down on him like a dove. A voice from heaven speaks to him: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”
passages.hearers:
Many Jews in Jesus' day felt that heaven had gone quiet. There had been no prophet like the old ones for centuries. A sky torn open, the Spirit coming down, and God's own voice speaking would have meant one thing: God is acting again.

The word Mark uses for the sky ‘breaking open’ is the Greek schizō, ‘to tear’. Mark uses it only one other time, near the end of his book, when the curtain of the temple is “torn in two from top to bottom” as Jesus dies (15:38). The book is bracketed by two tearings. At the start heaven is torn open over Jesus. At the end the curtain that hid God's presence is torn.
passages.ot:
The prophet Isaiah once prayed, “If only You would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). Mark shows that prayer being answered.

The voice's words echo two passages. Psalm 2:7 is God speaking to his chosen king: “You are My Son.” Isaiah 42:1 is God speaking of his servant, “in whom My soul delights.” In one sentence, Jesus is named both the king and the servant. The rest of Mark shows how he is both.

Some readers also hear Genesis 1:2 in the dove, where the Spirit of God hovers over the waters at creation, as though a new creation is beginning.
passages.hard: Why would Jesus need a baptism meant for turning from sin? Mark does not explain, and it is wise not to say more than he does. Christians have long read it as Jesus standing in line with sinners, taking his place beside the people he came to save. The voice from heaven makes clear that the problem is not his: God is “well pleased” with him. The notes below also take up whether the baptism made Jesus the Son of God or showed what he already was.
passages.asks: The Father says ‘beloved’ before Jesus has preached, healed, or done anything in public. Love comes first, before the work. Ask whether you live as though you must earn God's approval, or from a love already given.

passages.happening: At once the Spirit drives Jesus out into the desert. He stays forty days and is tested by Satan, the enemy of God. Mark adds two short details: he was with the wild animals, and angels served him. That is all Mark says. Matthew and Luke tell this scene at more length.
passages.hearers:
Forty is a number Jewish readers knew well. Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness, where God tested them (Deuteronomy 8:2). Moses was on the mountain forty days. Elijah walked forty days to the mountain of God (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus goes where Israel went and faces what Israel faced.

The Judean desert was a real and dangerous place: rock, heat, little water, and animals such as jackals and wild goats. ‘With the wild animals’ may simply mean he was alone and exposed. Some readers also hear a picture of peace with creation, like Adam in the garden before the fall.
passages.ot: Israel was tested in the wilderness and often failed. Adam was tested in a garden and fell. Here Jesus is tested in a wilderness, and Mark's short report suggests he stands. The angels who serve him recall God's care for Elijah, who was fed by an angel in the desert (1 Kings 19:5-8).
passages.hard: Why does Mark say the Spirit ‘drove’ Jesus out? The word is strong, the same one used later for driving out demons. It does not mean the Spirit was harsh. It means the test was part of God's plan, not an accident. Jesus did not wander into temptation. He was sent to face it.
passages.asks: Being close to God does not mean being kept from hard places. Right after the Father's ‘beloved’, Jesus is in the desert. Ask where you are being tested now, and whether you have assumed that the test means God has left you.

passages.happening: John is arrested. Jesus goes north to Galilee and starts to preach. His message is short: “The time is fulfilled,” he said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!” These are Jesus' first words in Mark, and they sum up everything he will do.
passages.hearers:
John's arrest was not a small matter. Mark later explains that Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, had John jailed because John spoke against his marriage (6:17). To start preaching just after that was to step into danger.

‘The kingdom of God’ was a phrase loaded with hope. For centuries Israel had been ruled by foreign empires: Babylon, Persia, the Greeks, and now Rome. Many longed for the day when God himself would reign, put things right, and set his people free. Jesus says that day has come near.

‘Gospel’ was also a public word. In the Roman world it was used for good news from the emperor, like a victory or the emperor's birthday. Jesus uses it for the news that God is king.
passages.ot: The prophets had promised that God would come to reign. Isaiah pictured a messenger running over the mountains with good news, saying to Zion, ‘Your God reigns’ (Isaiah 52:7). Daniel spoke of a kingdom the God of heaven would set up that would never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). Jesus says the waiting is over.
passages.asks: Jesus asks for two things: repent, which means turn around, and believe, which means trust the news. Turning without trusting becomes grim self-improvement. Trusting without turning changes nothing. Ask which of the two you find harder.

passages.happening: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon and Andrew, throwing a net into the water. He says, “Come, follow Me,” and, “I will make you fishers of men.” They leave their nets at once. A little farther on he calls two more brothers, James and John, who are mending nets in their father's boat. They leave their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and go.
passages.hearers:
The Sea of Galilee is a large freshwater lake, and fishing was a real trade there, not a hobby. In 1986, during a drought, two brothers found the remains of a fishing boat from about this time in the mud of the lake's shore. It was about eight metres long and had been patched many times. That is the kind of boat Mark has in mind.

Zebedee had hired men. That suggests a family business of some size. James and John were not leaving nothing. They were walking away from a trade, a father, and a future.

In Jesus' world, students usually chose a teacher and asked to follow him. Here the teacher chooses them. That reversal is itself a claim to authority.
passages.ot: The phrase ‘fishers of men’ may echo Jeremiah 16:16, where God says, “I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them.” In Jeremiah it is a picture of God gathering people, there for judgment. Jesus turns the picture into gathering people for the kingdom.
passages.asks: Mark tells this in four verses and gives no reasons, no long talk, no second thoughts. The call is simple and costly. Ask what nets you are holding: the things that are good in themselves but that you would find hard to leave if Jesus asked.

passages.happening: On the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, Jesus goes into the synagogue in Capernaum and teaches. People are stunned: he teaches with authority, not like the scribes. Then a man with an unclean spirit shouts at him. Jesus orders the spirit to be silent and come out. It throws the man into a fit and leaves with a scream. The crowd asks, “What is this? A new teaching with authority!”
passages.hearers:
A synagogue was the local meeting house, where Jews gathered on the Sabbath to read the Scriptures and pray. Visitors to Capernaum today see a handsome white stone synagogue, but that building is later. It is most often dated to the late 300s or 400s, though some scholars place it earlier. It stands on dark basalt foundations that some archaeologists date to the first century, possibly the floor of the synagogue Jesus knew.

The scribes were experts in the law of Moses. People expected a teacher to show where his teaching came from. Jesus speaks as if his own word is enough.

An ‘unclean spirit’ is Mark's usual name for a demon. In Jewish thinking, uncleanness was whatever made a person unfit to come near God's holy presence. A spirit that is unclean in a house of worship is a picture of evil sitting where God should be.
passages.ot: The spirit calls Jesus ‘the Holy One of God’. In the Old Testament, ‘the Holy One of Israel’ is one of God's own names, used again and again in Isaiah. The spirit knows who it is facing.
passages.hard: Was this a real evil spirit, or an illness people did not understand? Ancient people did know the difference between sickness and possession. Mark himself keeps them apart: in verse 34 Jesus heals ‘many who were ill’ and also ‘drove out many demons’. Christians today hold that evil is real and personal, while also using medicine for illness. Wisdom avoids both blaming every illness on demons and treating evil as a myth.
passages.asks: The crowd is amazed but not changed. They ask ‘What is this?’ and go home talking. The demon knows exactly who Jesus is and wants nothing to do with him. Knowing facts about Jesus is not the same as following him. Ask which you are doing.

passages.t: Healings at Simon's house and at the door
passages.happening: From the synagogue they go to the home of Simon and Andrew. Simon's mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus takes her hand and lifts her up. The fever goes, and she begins to serve them. That evening, after sunset, the whole town crowds round the door with their sick and troubled, and Jesus heals many and drives out many demons.
passages.hearers:
Why wait until sunset? The Jewish day ran from sunset to sunset, so the Sabbath ended at dusk. Carrying a load counted as work, and the prophet Jeremiah had forbidden carrying a load on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-22). Once the sun went down, people could carry their sick through the streets. Mark's small detail shows a town that kept the Sabbath and then came running.

In Capernaum, under a church built in the 400s, archaeologists found a house that early Christians honoured as Peter's. A pilgrim named Egeria wrote that she was shown Peter's house there in the late 300s. Whether it was truly his cannot be proved, but it shows how early the memory was kept.

The word for the woman's serving is the same Greek word Jesus uses for his own mission in 10:45: he came “to serve.” Only the angels in the desert have served Jesus before her (1:13). She is the first human being in Mark to do what Jesus came to do.
passages.asks: Jesus lifts the woman by the hand, and the first thing she does with her new strength is serve. Ask what you do with the strength God gives you.

passages.happening: Early the next morning, while it is still dark, Jesus slips away to a solitary place to pray. Simon and the others hunt for him. ‘Everyone is looking for you,’ they say. But Jesus will not go back to the crowds in Capernaum. He moves on to other towns, because preaching is why he came.
passages.hearers:
After a night of crowds and healing, any town in Galilee would have wanted Jesus to stay and set up as its healer. Simon's report sounds like good news. Jesus treats it as a temptation. He does not let success set his course.

The ‘solitary place’ is the same Greek word Mark used for the wilderness in verses 3, 4, 12 and 13. Jesus keeps going back to the place where he was tested.
passages.asks: Jesus prays before the day is busy and walks away from praise. Ask what sets the direction of your days: other people's demands, or time alone with God. And ask what ‘that is why I have come’ might mean for your own work.

passages.happening: A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus and begs, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” Jesus reaches out, touches him, and says, “I am willing,” and, “Be clean!” At once the disease leaves him. Jesus sends him to a priest to make the offering the law requires, and warns him to tell no one. The man tells everyone, and Jesus can no longer enter a town openly.
passages.hearers:
Biblical ‘leprosy’ was not the disease we now call leprosy (Hansen's disease). The Hebrew word covered a range of skin conditions, and even mould on cloth or walls. What made it terrible was not mainly pain. It was exclusion. The law told such a person to wear torn clothes, cover the face, cry ‘Unclean, unclean’, and live alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45-46). He could not worship with others, eat with his family, or be touched.

Touching an unclean person made you unclean too (Leviticus 5:3). So when Jesus touches the man, every hearer would expect Jesus to become unclean. Instead the flow runs the other way. Jesus' cleanness makes the man clean.

Only a priest could declare a person clean again and bring him back into the community (Leviticus 14). That is why Jesus sends him there. Jesus is not setting the law aside. He is giving the man his life back, and doing it through the proper door.
passages.ot: In the Old Testament, cleansing a leper was something only God could do. When a foreign general asked Israel's king to heal his leprosy, the king tore his clothes: “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” (2 Kings 5:7). Miriam was struck with the disease and healed only when Moses prayed (Numbers 12). Jesus cleanses with a touch and a word.
passages.hard:
Most manuscripts of verse 41 say Jesus was ‘moved with compassion’. One early manuscript, Codex Bezae, and a few old Latin copies say he was ‘moved with anger’. Some scholars think ‘anger’ is original, because a copyist would more likely soften it than invent it. If so, the anger was not at the man but at the disease and the misery it caused, much as Jesus was angry at hard hearts in 3:5. Either way, he touched him.

Why tell him to say nothing? Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder worker. The result proves the point: the news spreads, and Jesus can no longer go into the towns.
passages.asks: The man said, ‘If you are willing.’ He did not doubt Jesus' power. He doubted Jesus' wanting. Jesus answers that doubt first: ‘I am willing.’ Ask whether your trouble with God is about whether he can, or whether he cares.
